newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban face new attacks after north rout.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban face new attacks after north rout.

text.p: Afghan opposition factions counter-attacked Taleban militia in northeastern and central Afghanistan on Thursday after routing them in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghan sources in Pakistan said.
The Pakistani Foreign Ministry said it had information the purist Islamic militia were also engaged in peace talks with opponents in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Two Afghan opposition factions said they launched attacks against the Taleban north of the capital Kabul and in the central province of Bamiyan, and retaken three towns lost earlier this year.

A Taleban spokesman, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, confirmed fighting in the area but said an attack by forces led by renowned guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood was repulsed.
Fighting on the other front, in Bamiyan, was between the Taleban and a Shi'ite Moslem militia.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted sources in Masood's Jamiat-i-Islami faction as saying his forces attacked the Taleban frontline early on Thursday and later captured the towns of Golbahar, Jabal-os-Siraj and Charikar, all north of Kabul.

If confirmed, opposition capture of these areas would isolate Taleban forces who took the northeastern town of Pul-i-Khumri on Thursday after capturing the strategic Salang Pass on the main highway from Kabul to the north.
Reuters correspondent Tim Johnston reported from Pul-i-Khumri that the Taleban were in firm control of the town but there was fighting on the road to Mazar-i-Sharif, 160 km (100 miles) to the north.
AIP quoted Taleban sources in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar, which is the militia's headquarters, as saying only Golbahar had been attacked and the attackers were repelled.
There was no immediate independent account of the fighting, reported only a day after Taleban forces were forced to retreat from Mazar-i-Sharif which it capotured only last Saturday.

A Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters in Islamabad the Taleban were holding peace talks in Mazar-i-Sharif with their opponents, who drove the militia out on Thursday after an alliance struck a few days earlier collapsed.
The spokesman, quoting reports received in Islamabad, said "negotiations are currently under way in Afghanistan to remove differences among various groups".
He declined to give details, saying that would amount to interference in Afghan affairs.

Pakistan was the first country to recognise the Taleban government after the capture of Mazar-i-Sharif, the main opposition stronghold in the north previously held by the forces of northern opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Pakistan has a consulate in the city.

The spokesman said Pakistan had information "there were some differences" that led to the latest fighting in Mazar between the Taleban and Uzbek General Abdul Malik, who had defected from Dostum and allied himself with the militia.
"They are talking to each other now," he said.
Also involved in the talks was the opposition Hezb-i-Wahdat faction of Shi'ite Moslems, who fought alongside Malik's forces to drive the Taleban out of Mazar-i-Sharif.
